question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man, previously independent in all activities of daily living and followed only for well-controlled stage I hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, was rushed directly from the emergency department to the surgical intensive care unit thirty minutes after arriving from his assisted-living apartment with diffuse abdominal pain and rapidly progressive shortness of breath that began during breakfast. He does not smoke, has one glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, denies any history of malignancy, chronic lung disease, cirrhosis, organ transplantation, systemic corticosteroid use, or cytotoxic chemotherapy, and his medication list is limited to low-dose amlodipine and tamsulosin; his last clinic bloodwork six months earlier documented a hematocrit of 33 % and serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. He has never been told he has chronic kidney disease, chronic heart failure, chronic respiratory failure, or any other end-stage organ dysfunction, and he is not considered immunocompromised by any prior clinician. Emergency medical services found him sitting forward on the couch, clutching his left lower quadrant, breathing at a visibly rapid rate, and speaking in two- to three-word phrases; they applied a non-rebreather mask that was later measured in the resuscitation bay to deliver 55 % inspired oxygen but gave no intravenous fluids, analgesics, antibiotics, or vasopressors en route. On arrival—before any hospital therapy was initiated—manual blood pressure registered 112/60 mm Hg, radial pulse was regular at 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate counted for a full minute was 31 breaths per minute with pronounced accessory muscle recruitment, and temporal artery temperature read 37.6 °C. He opened his eyes to voice, answered orientation questions inconsistently, and followed simple commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 without sedatives on board. Skin examination revealed cool, clammy extremities but no cyanosis or mottling; capillary refill was roughly three seconds and jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Cardiac auscultation demonstrated a normal S1 and soft S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Pulmonary examination showed bibasilar crackles more prominent on the right with diminished breath sounds at both bases, but no wheezes. Abdominal inspection noted a distended, tympanitic lower abdomen; palpation elicited marked tenderness and voluntary guarding in the left iliac fossa with faint rebound, and bowel sounds were hypoactive. There was no flank ecchymosis and the liver edge was not palpable. Extremities displayed no edema; distal pulses were symmetric. A radial arterial blood gas drawn ten minutes after bed placement on the aforementioned oxygen concentration revealed a pH of 7.27, accompanying PaCO₂ of 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ of 94 mm Hg, and a calculated alveolar–arterial gradient of 321 mm Hg, confirming severe impairment in oxygen transfer out of proportion to the delivered fraction of inspired oxygen. Simultaneously obtained laboratory studies demonstrated serum sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.3 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, glucose 124 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL—slightly above his known baseline but without oliguria in the preceding twelve hours according to assisted-living records; overall urine output has remained well above 0.5 mL/kg/h, so formal criteria for acute kidney injury are not fulfilled. Complete blood count showed white blood cell count 14 500 /mm³ with 89 % neutrophils, hematocrit 29 %, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, and platelets 218 000 /µL; mean corpuscular volume was 88 fL. Serum lactate returned at 3.1 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin was negative and coagulation studies were within normal limits. A supine abdominal radiograph obtained before any analgesia or antibiotics displayed multiple distended colonic loops with air-fluid levels and free intraperitoneal air under the right hemidiaphragm, while a portable chest film demonstrated patchy bilateral opacities suggestive of early acute lung injury rather than cardiogenic edema; the cardiothoracic ratio remained normal. Focused bedside ultrasound revealed a hyperdynamic left ventricle, a collapsible inferior vena cava with greater than 50 % respiratory variation, and trace perisplenic free fluid. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 100 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no ischemic changes. Bladder scan indicated 120 mL of clear yellow urine, and a Foley catheter inserted in the bay yielded another 40 mL a few minutes later. Blood cultures, serum amylase, lipase, and C-reactive protein were drawn but results were pending at the moment of ICU transfer. No crystalloid bolus, antibiotic dose, vasopressor infusion, or endotracheal intubation had been started prior to the documentation of the above physiologic and laboratory data, ensuring that the vital signs of 112/60 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute, temperature 37.6 °C, respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute, pH 7.27, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.3 mmol/L, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, hematocrit 29 %, white blood cell count 14 500 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 55 %, and alveolar–arterial gradient 321 mm Hg represent his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums 12 acute physiology components, age points, and chronic health points. Using the documented admission values:
- Vital signs: Temperature 37.6 °C = 0; mean arterial pressure (112 + 2 × 60)/3 = 77.3 mm Hg = 0; heart rate 102/min = 0; respiratory rate 31/min (25–34) = 1.
- Gas exchange and pH: FiO₂ is 0.55, so use the A–a gradient rather than PaO₂. Gradient 321 mm Hg (200–349) = 2; arterial pH 7.27 (7.25–7.32) = 2.
- Chemistry: Sodium 133 mmol/L = 0; potassium 5.3 mmol/L = 0; creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (1.5–1.9) = 2, without doubling because acute renal failure is absent.
- Blood counts and neurologic status: Hematocrit 29% (20–29.9%) = 2; WBC 14,500/mm³ = 0; GCS 13 gives 15 − 13 = 2.
Acute physiology subtotal = 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 2 = 11. Age 74 (65–74) adds 5; no qualifying chronic organ failure or immunocompromise adds 0.
Total = 11 + 5 + 0 = 16.
Final answer: 16
